title: Beavers: Tail Slapping Fun
summary: Josh and Chuck explore beavers: the two living species (American and Eurasian), their size, the tail's uses and tail-slapping warning, underwater adaptations, family life in lodges, and how they build dams that create wetlands. They cover the ecological benefits (water filtration, nitrogen removal, flood control, aquifer recharge, fire breaks, habitat for other animals), the conflicts with timber and farm owners and humane mitigation such as beaver deceivers and flow devices, castoreum and its uses, the testicle myth, the sixteenth-century papal fish ruling, and rare beaver attacks. The episode closes with a listener mail about the Braver Angels depolarization organization.

segments.title: Opening banter and beaver introduction
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about the episode's Orange Incisors theme, rodents in general, and tie beavers to earlier episodes on porcupines and wetlands.

segments.title: Beaver species and size
segments.summary: The two living beaver species, American and Eurasian, are described, including weight, length, and where they live. Their range was reduced by overhunting for fur.

segments.title: Beaver tail and swimming adaptations
segments.summary: The beaver's tail works as a rudder, propeller, and kickstand, and beavers slap it on water as a warning. Adaptations for swimming include webbed feet, sealable ears and nose, nictitating membranes, and breath-holding of about fifteen minutes.

segments.title: Keystone species role
segments.summary: Beavers are described as a keystone species whose presence increases biodiversity and whose removal reduces it.

segments.title: Beaver lodges and family life
segments.summary: Lodges are domed structures with underwater entrances. Beaver families are monogamous, live with their kits, and young beavers stay until about two before building their own lodge. Beavers are mostly nocturnal and do not hibernate.

segments.title: How beavers build dams and maintain them
segments.summary: Beavers build dams from mud, gravel, sticks, and trees, flooding dry land to create wetlands. Families work together, and they inspect and patch dams regularly. Teeth contain iron and stay sharp while gnawing, and beavers can digest cellulose.

segments.title: Environmental benefits of beaver dams
segments.summary: Beaver wetlands filter sediment, handle farm fertilizer runoff via nitrogen removal, prevent erosion, flood control, recharge aquifers, and create fire breaks. Many animals benefit, including invertebrates, birds, ducks, woodpeckers, and moose.

segments.title: Beaver conflicts with humans and mitigation
segments.summary: Timber owners and road builders lose money to beaver flooding. Mitigation methods include beaver pipes, pre-dams, beaver deceivers at culverts, chicken wire, and anti-gnaw paint. The hosts argue that many conflicts are only problems because of human plans.
